source.title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
source.authors: Cheng Jin; Zhong-Tian Ma; Xiao Wang; Han Qi; Xiaoyu Wen; Xiang Wang; You-Bang Sun; Xia Hu; Bo-Wen Zhou; Chao-Chao Lu; Qiao-Sheng Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study compares parameter-level unlearning and a new architectural method, and directly tests how their WMDP results change under standard post-training. It finds substantial rebounds for many baselines but smaller or no rebounds for REX.
record.gate_note: The study tests one standard 250M-token fine-tuning trajectory, not the other proposed attacks. Fine-tuning results cited from earlier work are not recorded as rows. The reported WMDP values before and after fine-tuning are included in the relevant rows; the study does not report an activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery test.
record.test_reason: Applies one shared 250M-token benign SFT to nine parameter-level unlearning baselines and to REX on three MoE models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Intern-S2, Gemma-4-26B-A4B), reporting WMDP before and after. The SFT is an instruction mix with the life-science subsets removed, run once with one data order and seed. Of the nine baselines, 4 to 7 per setting are usable. Baselines that reached low or moderate WMDP rebound toward the fine-tuned original, which challenges A and bears on B. REX is offered as a counter-method whose delivered model rebounds far less (F). A direct-SFT control shows where that robustness does not hold.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that REX relocates hazardous knowledge into removable experts and, on the base model, matches the strongest of nine parameter-level baselines while largely keeping general capability. After one standard 250M-token SFT, the delivered model has the lowest WMDP of all usable methods in all six settings, while parameter-level baselines rebound toward the fine-tuned original. The paraphrase should add that this durability comes from fine-tuning the recombined full model and excising at delivery: fine-tuning the excised model directly ends 9.6-20.2 points higher on Bio.
record.recipe_differences: REX adds target experts to pretrained MoE models, uses selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, excises the new experts, and applies RMU cleanup. It tests standard post-training as a recovery procedure rather than reproducing an original unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by backbone and domain. The study reports one shared 250M-token SFT trajectory; Bio and Cyber have different relocation corpora and budgets. REX's post-SFT WMDP rebound ranges from a slight decrease to a substantial increase across settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying the RMU cleanup alone to the original model (R) lowers WMDP-Bio, yet bio-adjacent MMLU subjects stay high: 85.8 for R versus 68.2 for A2 on Intern-S2. The authors read this as suppression of benchmark answers rather than removal of knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter-level unlearning lowers target-benchmark scores while adjacent-domain knowledge persists, indicating suppression rather than deletion.

record.problems: The standard post-training comparison uses one shared data order and seed; the main WMDP results have no reported error bars. Only one SFT recipe and trajectory are tested. The text reports standard-deviation results for a five-seed random-expert-excision control, but that is not replication of the main recovery comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported SFT endpoint results bearing on A or B were left out. Table 1 general-capability comparisons after SFT and the remaining general benchmarks are not separately rowed; the selected Table 2 MMLU rows document base-model capability retention. Table 11's random-expert-excision control is not included because it is not a recovery attack or one of the named claim versions.

untested.parts: Quantization, activation-direction edits, prompting attacks and adversarial fine-tuning on hazardous data. Only one benign SFT is run (250M tokens, life-science subsets removed, one seed).

Small relearning sets, relearning on a subset of the forgotten facts, and loosely related data. Only one large unrelated instruction SFT is tested, with a single seed. The intermediate 10M to 100M checkpoints appear only in a figure.
No activation-direction ablation and no probe of access versus deletion. The only related analysis (RMU cleanup leaves bio-adjacent MMLU high) is recorded under fits_no_version.
REX is not tested against adversarial fine-tuning on hazardous data, activation ablation, quantization or prompting attacks, nor with more than one SFT recipe or seed.

missing.what: Matched RMU control R-SFT (REX's RMU cleanup settings applied to the original model, then the same SFT). Bio: 41.6 to 78.8, 33.3 to 81.0, 48.5 to 71.5. Cyber: 31.8 to 43.5, 30.9 to 44.7, 30.9 to 37.6. RMU removal from near chance is undone by benign SFT.
The same R-SFT control as a recovery measurement: under the shared SFT, Bio rises 23.0-47.7 points and Cyber 6.7-13.8 points.
WMDP trajectories at 10M, 50M and 100M SFT tokens, showing how fast baselines rebound. Figure only, no numbers in the text.
The full model F3 keeps the hazardous knowledge, ending 2.3-6.0 WMDP points below the original+SFT. REX therefore separates the knowledge into removable experts rather than deleting it.
Bio-adjacent MMLU subjects (15% of questions) fall 20.0-21.7 points from B to A2, while the other subjects fall 1.2-2.8. After SFT, A3's adjacent subjects reach 66.5-76.8 against 81.5-88.7 for B.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Every row r1-r47 now has its own row_fixes item with declared letters; the earlier 'same applies to' items are expanded. Mapping was decided by what each row measures: parameter-level baselines get A and B, REX delivered and A3-direct rows get B and F, and REX capability rows get F.
(2) Row states follow the catalog convention of measuring recovery (the shallowness effect), so for F low recovery means the method holds.
(3) r27 changed from observed to partial (kept share 34%, as for r30 and r22). r36-r38 changed from observed to partial (49-64% recovered, consistent with r22).
(4) r20, r23, r25 and r32 (moderate removals with small rebounds) are now itemized. They get their own A limits_scope and B limits_scope labels, and r25 and r32 move out of the Cyber challenges label. That label's earlier reason was wrong: Qwen PDU keeps about 80% and Gemma NPO 64%, not at most 63%.
(5) r22 was in no B label and is now in the B incomplete-rebound label. The B A3-direct label changed from supports to limits_scope and now includes r39-r41.
(6) The F labels are split into separate condition groups. r42-r44 no longer sit in both F supports and F limits_scope, and r39-r41 are added to the A3-direct label.
(7) test_reason now gives 4 to 7 usable baselines per setting instead of 7.
(8) Missing entries now each name one version: the R-SFT control is split into A and B entries, and a Table 13 entry is added.
Caveats: the SFT is benign (instruction mix, life-science subsets removed) and run once with one seed and no error bars on the main comparisons, so F's robustness is shown only against developer-style post-training. Seven Bio baseline conditions made no or mostly non-specific removal (Table 2), so they cannot show recovery. Before any SFT, most usable baselines already sit far above chance (Table 2), which limits A independently of recovery. Method and hyperparameter tables were skimmed rather than parsed in full. The text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests WMDP reduction, general-capability retention, and recovery under its standard fine-tuning procedure. It does not test quantization, internal activation edits, or prompting-only attacks.

Tests one 250M-token standard instruction fine-tuning procedure. Does not vary the fine-tuning data size or test unrelated/loosely related examples as separate conditions, nor fine-tuning on a subset of forgotten facts.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether an unlearning method merely blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context-information recovery test.
REX is tested against standard fine-tuning only, not against internal edits, quantization, or prompting attacks.
